planting.note: Scarify the hard seed coat lightly and sow in fall or early spring into well-drained, dry, sandy or clay-loam soil in full sun; plains poppy mallow forms a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established, so sow it where it is to grow.

directions: Direct sow into well-drained, dry soil in full sun; plains poppy mallow is a sprawling Great Plains and south-central native with deeply lobed leaves and cup-shaped, rich wine-red to magenta flowers held above the foliage on wiry stems from spring through early summer. A thick taproot makes established plants extremely drought tolerant and essentially impossible to move successfully, so choose a permanent, well-drained location before sowing rather than planning to transplant later. The trailing stems weave attractively through low grasses and other prairie perennials without smothering them, making it an excellent component of a naturalistic prairie or meadow planting rather than a tidy formal border. It needs no supplemental fertilizer or irrigation once established and self-sows modestly in open, undisturbed soil.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or early spring into lean, well-drained, dry, sandy soil in full sun; pale evening primrose spreads by rhizomes in loose, sandy ground and naturalizes readily once established.

directions: Direct sow into lean, sharply drained, sandy soil in full sun; pale evening primrose is a low, spreading native of dry plains and sandy desert grassland, with narrow gray-green leaves and large, satiny white flowers that open in late afternoon and evening, fading to pale pink as they age the following day. The fragrant, moth-pollinated blooms make it a valuable addition to an evening or moon garden, where the pale flowers glow in low light and draw sphinx moths and other night-flying pollinators. It spreads by shallow, creeping rhizomes to form a loose colony in loose, sandy soil, tolerating extreme heat, drought, and poor fertility better than nearly any bedding annual. Avoid rich soil and heavy irrigation, which encourage floppy, less floriferous growth in this drought-adapted plains native.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into average, well-drained soil in full sun; golden-wave coreopsis germinates with fall rains, overwinters as a low rosette, and blooms in a spring flush alongside bluebonnets and Indian paintbrush.

directions: Direct sow into average, well-drained soil in full sun in fall; golden-wave coreopsis is one of the signature annual wildflowers of Texas roadside displays, forming dense drifts of bright golden-yellow, maroon-centered daisy flowers over finely divided foliage from mid to late spring. Seedlings overwinter as low rosettes and bolt quickly into bloom once spring warmth arrives, often carpeting whole fields and roadsides in a solid sheet of yellow for several weeks. It self-sows abundantly in undisturbed, sunny soil, so once established in a compatible site it typically returns reliably for years without replanting. Allow seed heads to fully mature and shatter before mowing or clearing spent plants, and avoid heavy mulch, which can interfere with the light-dependent germination this native annual needs.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring into lean, well-drained, dry soil in full sun; prairie verbena spreads by trailing, rooting stems to form a dense, low mat and is among the most common native verbenas of Texas roadsides and prairies.

directions: Direct sow into lean, well-drained, dry soil in full sun; prairie verbena forms a low, spreading mat of finely divided, ferny leaves topped almost continuously from spring through fall with rounded clusters of small lavender-purple flowers that draw butterflies in large numbers. It is one of the most common and durable native groundcover wildflowers of the southern Great Plains, coloring roadsides, prairies, and disturbed ground with a long-lasting purple haze through the growing season. Trailing stems root as they spread, quickly filling in bare, sunny ground and tolerating foot traffic and mowing far better than most flowering perennials, which makes it a good choice between stepping stones or as an informal lawn substitute in hot, dry sites. It is extremely drought tolerant once established and needs no supplemental fertilizer, blooming most heavily in lean, unimproved soil.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring into lean, well-drained, dry, rocky or sandy, alkaline soil in full sun; Berlandier's sundrops is named for the distinctly square, four-angled flower buds that precede its bright yellow blooms.

directions: Direct sow into lean, sharply drained, dry, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; Berlandier's sundrops is a low, mounding Texas and south-central native with narrow leaves and abundant bright, lemon-yellow, four-petaled flowers that open in late afternoon and remain open into the following morning, unlike some evening primrose relatives that close by midday. Distinctive squared-off flower buds give the plant its common name and are visible even before the blooms open, adding subtle interest to the low mounding form. It blooms over an extended season from late spring through fall in favorable conditions, drawing bees and occasional sphinx moths at dusk. Extremely drought tolerant and long-lived in lean, rocky soil, it is well suited to rock gardens, dry slopes, and xeriscape borders where richer, moister conditions would shorten its life and reduce flowering.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring into lean, well-drained, dry, rocky or gravelly, alkaline soil in full sun; yellow prairie flax is a short-lived, wiry-stemmed Texas Hill Country and Edwards Plateau native that self-seeds readily.

directions: Direct sow into lean, sharply drained, rocky or gravelly soil in full sun; yellow prairie flax is a slender, wiry-stemmed native wildflower of Texas limestone hills and prairies, with fine, needle-like leaves and small, bright golden-yellow, five-petaled flowers that open fresh each morning and shatter by afternoon, replaced by a new flush of blooms the following day over a long spring and early summer season. Individual plants are short-lived, typically persisting only a couple of seasons, but self-sow readily in lean, undisturbed, rocky soil to maintain a naturalized population over time. Its fine, airy texture works well threaded through a rock garden or dry prairie planting among bunchgrasses and other low, drought-tolerant wildflowers rather than as a stand-alone specimen. Avoid rich soil, mulch, and regular irrigation, which shorten its already brief lifespan and reduce self-sowing.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring into lean, well-drained, dry, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; red dome blanketflower is a compact Southwest native adapted to desert grassland and dry mesas, more finely textured than the common bedding blanketflower.

directions: Direct sow into lean, sharply drained, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; red dome blanketflower is a compact Southwestern desert grassland native with finely cut, grayish-green leaves and cheerful yellow, red-based flowers surrounding a domed reddish-brown center, blooming over a long season from late spring through fall in response to warm-season rainfall. It is more finely textured and lower-growing than the widely sold hybrid bedding blanketflowers, with a wiry, deep-rooted habit suited to harsh, dry, exposed sites where richer garden perennials fail. Deadheading extends the bloom season, though the plant reseeds readily on its own in lean, undisturbed soil, often naturalizing into a self-sustaining colony over a few years. It tolerates intense heat, reflected sun, and extended drought once established, needing no supplemental irrigation beyond occasional deep watering in the harshest dry spells.
